scenes.title: hook: one tendency behind every test

voiceover.text: Last time, every metal that reacted in our tests did the same thing. It turned into positive ions, and to do that, it lost electrons. So a reactive metal is one that gives its outer electrons away easily. Potassium gives them up in an instant, while gold hangs on to them. But why should one metal let go more easily than another? A big part of the answer is inside the atom.

scenes.title: down a group: further out, easier off

voiceover.text: You've met part of the answer with the alkali metals. Going down Group one, from lithium to sodium to potassium, each atom has one more shell, so the outer electron sits further from the nucleus. The core charge stays the same, so that distant electron is held less tightly. The first ionisation energy, the energy to pull it off, falls from five hundred and twenty, to four hundred and ninety-six, to four hundred and nineteen kilojoules per mole. Less energy needed means the metal loses that electron more readily, so reactivity rises down the group.

scenes.title: across a period: a tighter grip

voiceover.text: Now go across Period three: sodium, magnesium, aluminium. Sodium fizzes hard in cold water, magnesium barely reacts, and aluminium shows no change at all, partly because of a surface layer we'll come back to. Across the period, each atom has one more proton, but its outer electrons stay in the same shell. So the core charge rises, from one, to two, to three, and the atom gets smaller. Both changes pull the outer electrons in tighter, so they're harder to remove.

scenes.title: a surprise in the data (countdown, 3 seconds)

voiceover.text: But here's a surprise. Aluminium's first ionisation energy is five hundred and seventy-eight, lower than magnesium's seven hundred and thirty-eight. So why isn't aluminium more reactive than magnesium? Think about the ions they form. Quick prediction. How many electrons does each atom have to lose?

scenes.title: the whole job, not the first step

voiceover.text: Sodium loses one electron, magnesium loses two, and aluminium loses three. Each extra electron comes off a smaller, more positive ion, so it costs more. Add up the whole job, and sodium needs four hundred and ninety-six kilojoules per mole, magnesium about two thousand two hundred, and aluminium over five thousand. The whole job gets harder across the period, and that's a big part of why reactivity falls from sodium to aluminium.

The syllabus names one more property, electronegativity. That's how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons it shares in a bond. Line up the metals in the activity series, and their electronegativity climbs as you go down the list, from potassium at zero point eight two, up to gold at two point five four. An atom with a weak pull on shared electrons also holds its own outer electrons weakly. Both numbers come from the same thing underneath, how tightly the nucleus grips its outer electrons.

So here's the chain to use in an answer. A larger atom, or a lower core charge, means a weaker grip on the outer electrons. That gives a lower ionisation energy and a lower electronegativity, so the metal loses electrons more easily, and it's more reactive. In short, weaker grip, easier loss, more reactive. Notice what the chain doesn't mention. It isn't about how many electrons a metal has. Gold has seventy-nine electrons, potassium has only nineteen, and gold is far less reactive.

These trends help explain the patterns down a group and across a period. But the grip is never the whole story. What happens to the ions once they're in water matters too, and when you compare metals from different parts of the table, like iron and copper, it can decide the order. That's why the activity series is built from measured reactions, not worked out from atoms alone.

Now back to aluminium. Its place in the series says it should be more reactive than zinc, yet the foil hardly reacted in acid. Aluminium reacts with oxygen in the air so readily that its surface is instantly covered by a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide. That layer sticks tightly and keeps water and acid away from the metal. Protection by an oxide layer like this is called passivation. It's why aluminium window frames and drink cans last for years.

Here's a classic demonstration, shown as footage. Aluminium foil sits in blue copper sulfate solution, and almost nothing happens. Then some sodium chloride, ordinary salt, is stirred in. Chloride ions break up the oxide layer, and soon the foil fizzes, the mixture gets hot, and brown copper forms. Same metal, same copper ions. Breaking the protective layer let the aluminium react, so the slow start was never low reactivity.

So keep two ideas apart. A metal's underlying tendency to lose electrons sets its place in the series. The grip of its atoms is part of that tendency, and measured reactions fix the place. What you see in one test also depends on the surface, the size of the piece and the conditions. Sodium's dull tarnish slowed its start in water, and aluminium's oxide hides its tendency far more completely.
Your turn. Calcium is more reactive than magnesium. Explain why, using atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity. Pause here to answer.

Calcium's outer electrons are in a fourth shell, so the atom is larger, and they're further from the nucleus with the same core charge. They're held less tightly, so calcium has the lower ionisation energy, and the lower electronegativity. It loses its two outer electrons more easily. Saying calcium has more electrons to lose is the slip. Each atom loses just two.

Last one. A student finds that aluminium foil reacts more slowly with dilute acid than zinc does, and concludes that aluminium is less reactive than zinc. Evaluate this conclusion. Pause here to answer.

The conclusion is wrong. Aluminium is above zinc in the measured activity series, so a clean aluminium surface reacts more readily. The foil was slow because its oxide layer kept the acid off at first. Once that layer breaks down, aluminium reacts vigorously. Ranking a metal by a slow start, without checking its surface, is the trap.

So reactivity trends follow how easily a metal's atoms lose their outer electrons. But those electrons don't just vanish. When zinc went into copper sulfate, each zinc atom lost two electrons, and each copper ion picked two up. One can't happen without the other. Chemists have names for those two halves, and a way to track electrons even when no ions are visible. How do electron transfer and oxidation number identify redox?
